bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues lower policy support by about .06 (study 1, p < .01, N = 747), about .07 (study 2, no p-value stated in the text) and about .07 in the pooled studies 1-4 meta-analysis (no p-value stated). In-party cues add about .03, non-significant in studies 1 and 2 and reported without a test in the pooled model. The out-party sign is negative, so the paper supports no positive out-partisan persuasion weight.
bearings.paper_location: Study 1 p.1065; study 2 p.1066; meta-analysis pp.1070-1071, Table 4 and app. E.2
bearings.system_side: cpf_pressure in fec/moneyball_core.py returns 1.7 for co-partisan pairs, 0.5 for cross-party D/R pairs and 1.0 otherwise; the docstring at line 11 cites Furnas/Bakker source-alignment. fec/engine/flip_model.py line 58 binds it, and lines 138-139 sum pro-campaign neighbours into nA and anti neighbours into nB, both weighted by cpf, so an out-party pro-CU neighbour adds positive pull at weight 0.5. The dashboard align() at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl line 585 returns SRCPRO/SRCANTI; the constant values were not checked.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Direction only. The paper measures mass-public 0-1 policy support after one embedded cue, on low-salience issues, in 2016-2018 non-probability online panels. It does not measure legislator-to-legislator pressure, cosponsorship or lobbying. The sign result supports zeroing or reversing the out-partisan weight, not the 1.7 amplification, since the paper's in-party effect is small and often null. Legislator-side constants need elite cue evidence such as Box-Steffensmeier et al.
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers and page locations verified against the text. 'Significant' is stated only for study 1; study 2 and the pooled out-party estimate carry no test in the text, so the rel summary's 'significant repulsion' is overstated. The 1.7 and 0.5 constants do not come from this paper; the relation holds only for the positive 0.5 out-partisan weight.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues lower policy support by about .07 on a 0-1 scale in the pooled studies 1-4 analysis, relative to the no-cue control. The paper does not use the word backfire; the decrease is the reported effect. Heterogeneity runs through partisan identity strength interacted with cognitive resources (NfC, latent resources). The paper measures no bipartisan-bridge or cross-party attribute. The authors say real messages often carry both in-party and out-party cues.
bearings.paper_location: Meta-analysis pp.1070-1071 and Table 4; discussion p.1074
bearings.system_side: BAKKER_XCUE defaults to on (fec/engine/lt_priming.py line 63, env default '1'). xf(u,v) at line 64 returns 1.0 for same-party pairs and sqrt(bpf_u times bpf_v) for cross-party pairs, so a cross-party pro-cue is scaled by bridge share and is never negative. xf is applied in the pressure sum (line 103) and in the recruit candidate terms (lines 131 and 133). The dashboard port at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl line 630 mirrors it.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Sign only. The paper supports shrinking out-party cross-cues toward zero, which the bpf scaling does. The paper does not support the bridge exemption, under which sqrt(bpf) restores full cross-party influence for perfect bridge pairs, because bipartisanship is never measured. Mass-public one-shot survey effects do not transfer to elite cosponsorship recruitment without elite-level evidence.
bearings.verifier_note: The 'null-to-backfire' comment at lt_priming.py:57 is confirmed. 'Backfire' is an interpretive label for a reported decrease. The rel's 'usually' should read 'often' per p.1074. The claim that heterogeneity is not through a bridge attribute holds only because the paper measures no such attribute. The bridge exemption is the rel's own concern and is not supported by the paper.

bearings.paper_claim: Out-party cues lower support by about .06 to .07 and in-party cues raise it by about .03 (pooled and studies 1-2). The authors speculate, post hoc, that in-party patterns were stronger in the food irradiation (change) studies and out-party patterns in the farm subsidy (status quo) studies, and name other possible explanations.
bearings.system_side: salience_shock.py steps_for (lines 99-111): the retreat regime gives co-partisans +1 and out-partisans -1; rally gives co-partisans +1 and out-partisans +0.5 only when bpf is at least 0.30; backfire gives out-partisans -1. These are sign-and-unit steps before intensity and susceptibility scaling. The dashboard efm() at make_dashboard_html_00.tpl lines 659-660 applies the oppose and support multipliers, and its comment at lines 655-656 cites Lee 2009, not Bakker or Furnas.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's mass-level out-party repulsion supports the negative out-partisan step in retreat and backfire. It shows no positive out-party movement, so it does not back the rally +0.5 step, which must rest on other sources. The issue-dependence finding is post hoc and should not be used to select a regime.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper claims and page locations verified. The rel's statement that the brain attributes the execMode oppose behaviour to Bakker and Furnas is not in the code, which cites Lee 2009; the brain was not read, so that attribution is unverified. The rel's sign-and-unit description omits intensity and susceptibility scaling.

bearings.paper_claim: Cue receptivity is not higher among low-resource people; the meta-analysis shows no larger cue effects for low resources. Among high-resource respondents the in-party cue effect rises with partisan identity strength: meta slopes CRT b=.09 (SE .04), NfC b=.15 (SE .05), latent b=.15 (SE .05). The roughly 15-percentage-point rise from lowest to highest identity strength is reported for latent resources only.
bearings.paper_location: Meta-analysis pp.1070-1071 and Figure 3; abstract p.1061
bearings.system_side: receptivity_layer.py lines 173-191: susc_trait = .40 cooperation_v2 + .30 N - .20 diligence - .10 dominance (line 186), described in the module docstring (lines 6-9) as a design prior and not a Byrne finding. The final susceptibility is (1 minus PW) times susc_trait plus PW times the persona z, with PW from PERSONA_W defaulting to 0.30 (line 147). The persona z uses communion and agency, not partisan identity, so the layer has no partisan identity strength term. cooperation_v2 is a cross-party share that the file notes is near-duplicate of bpf (rho +0.888).
bearings.transfer_conditions: Weak. The paper studies the mass public; legislators are high-resource and strongly identified, so the moderator has little range in Congress. The paper concerns party cues, not lobbying pressure. The layer's design prior does not come from this paper. UNVERIFIED agent analysis (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: The rel's formula omits the 30 percent persona blend in the final susceptibility. The 15-point figure applies to latent resources only. The gap claim that no partisan identity term exists is verified.

summary_issues: summary_md calls the out-party decrease a significant repulsion. The paper gives p-values only for study 1 (p < .01); study 2 and the pooled -.07 are stated without tests.
summary_md says the 15-point rise applies to slopes of .15 for NfC and latent resources. The paper states the 15-point figure for latent resources only.
gaps_exposed says no component has a negative out-party term. salience_shock.py retreat and backfire regimes give out-partisans -1, so the claim holds only for cpf_pressure and lt_priming.

gaps_exposed says bpf is the only identity variable in the engine. The receptivity layer also uses a communion and agency persona z (PERSONA_W 0.30) and the cooperation share, and party is the categorical identity. The claim should be narrowed.
